title: Who does what?
bubbles: Have you cleaned the bathroom yet?
sources: SB p.30–31 (PDF 31–32), Grammar Bank p.132–133 (PDF 133–134), Vocabulary Bank p.154 (PDF 155), Communication p.104/106 (PDF 105/107), scripts p.121 (PDF 122); WB p.26–27 (PDF 25–26), key WB p.89 (PDF 89)

reference.title: The Lazy Person’s Guide to a clean and tidy home
rows: Ten minutes twice a day – set an alarm on your phone.
Keep cleaning products in the right place.
Near the place where you need them: bathroom cleaners in the bathroom, bin bags by the bin.
Water and half a lemon in a bowl, three minutes on high, then wipe with a cloth.
Use your dishwasher to clean other things.
Tell people to take off their shoes when they come in.
If they refuse, give them the vacuum cleaner!
Use your socks to clean the floor.
On a hard floor (wood or stone); then put your socks in the washing machine.
Listen to music while you clean.
Especially for housework you hate, like ironing.

reference.title: Talking about housework
reference.text: Who does the most housework in your house? What housework do you hate doing? What don’t you mind doing? Have you done any housework today? We say do housework, do the cleaning, do sport – not make housework.

tasks.instruction: Read the headlines. The same word is missing in each one. What is it?
tasks.note: SB 1a+1b (проверка по статьям) → Blank; ответ по тексту статей (MODEL)
tasks.context: 1 Doing ___ is as good as going to the gym. Doing exercise for 30 minutes a day is good for your health, a new Canadian study has found. The study looked at 130,000 people in 17 countries. Only 3% of the people did 30 minutes of sport a day, like running or swimming. But the researchers found that you don’t need to do sport or go to the gym – any form of physical activity is good for you, including housework. Activities like doing the cleaning are really good exercise, so you can stay healthy and have a clean house at the same time. 2 NEW SPANISH LAW: children must help their parents with ___. Is it a battle to get your kids to help with housework? Think about moving to live in Spain, where the government has decided that children under the age of 18, both boys and girls, have an obligation to ‘participate in family life’ – and that includes doing housework. However, they don’t say what happens to children who say no when their parents ask them to do something.

exercises.situation: You are a classmate in an English class (level: pre-intermediate). You talk about housework. Ask the student, one at a time: Do men and women in your country both do housework? Who does more? Is this fair? How much housework do teenagers do? Who does the most housework in your house or flat? Is everyone happy with this? What housework do you do? How often? What housework do you hate doing? What don’t you mind doing? Do you ever find housework relaxing? Have you done any housework today? What? Give short answers about yourself too (you hate ironing, you don’t mind cooking, you did the washing-up this morning). Use do / make + housework phrases naturally. If the student says make the housework or makes a mistake with the present perfect (I have cleaned yesterday), repeat the correct form naturally.
exercises.goal: Talk about who does the housework and what you like doing.
exercises.opener: Hi! Let’s talk about housework. Who does the most housework in your house?

reference.title: make or do?
reference.text: We usually use do for activities and work: do housework, do the cleaning, do homework, do sport. We usually use make when we create or produce something: make lunch, make a noise, make a mistake, make plans. Housework phrases often use do + the + -ing: do the ironing, do the washing-up.

reference.wrong: I make the housework at the weekend.
reference.right: I do the housework at the weekend.

reference.title: Present perfect
rows: I have not / He has not
Yes, I have. / No, he hasn’t.

reference.title: When do we use it?
reference.text: Form: have / has + past participle. We use the present perfect for finished actions in the recent past, connected to now, when we don’t say exactly when: I’ve cleaned the fridge – it looks new! We also use it to give news: Mary’s had her baby! A parcel has arrived for you. Regular past participles = past simple (-ed): cleaned, finished. Irregular: done, made, been, broken, come, put (Irregular verbs p.164).

reference.title: yet, just, already
rows: at the end of ? and − sentences
Have you finished your homework yet? No, not yet. I haven’t finished yet.
before the main verb in + sentences = a very short time ago
My sister’s just started a new job.
before the main verb in + sentences = sooner than expected
No, I’ve already seen it three times.

reference.wrong: I’ve cleaned the fridge ten minutes ago.
reference.right: I cleaned the fridge ten minutes ago.
reference.why: With an exact time (ten minutes ago, yesterday) use the past simple, not the present perfect.

reference.right: He’s made lunch. = He has made lunch.

exercises.explain: he / she / it + has.

Have you done the ironing yet?
exercises.explain: Present perfect with already / yet: Have you… done…?

reference.title: y and j at the beginning of words

reference.text: At the beginning of a word y is pronounced /j/ (like the y in you) and j is pronounced /dʒ/ (like the j in jazz). Don’t pronounce yet like jet!
